Machine learning · chapter 1.6c · prototype methods

Prototype Methods & Adaptive Nearest Neighbours

A few well-placed points can speak for the whole training set

Nearest neighbours (chapter 1.6) keeps every training point and compares each new case with all of them. Prototype methods keep only a handful of labelled points, the prototypes, and give a new case the label of the closest one. The space splits into cells, one per prototype, and the classifier is simply the colour of the cell you land in. This chapter is about where to put the prototypes, and about choosing a better notion of “closest”: one that ignores a slightly rotated digit, or that stretches along a class boundary. On the right are 120 training points from three classes and nine prototypes, three per class. Drag any prototype (the large outlined dots) and watch the cells and the mistakes change.

The idea
Store a few labelled prototypes; label a new point by the nearest one
Better distances
Tangent distance shrugs off small shifts and turns; DANN stretches along the boundary
In practice
Handwriting, satellite images and any problem with a good measure of similarity

The idea

Prototypes: k-means as a classifier

The methods in this chapter are model-free: they assume almost nothing about how the classes are shaped, so they can follow very irregular boundaries. The price is that they explain little. You get good predictions, not a formula you can read. They are best used as accurate black boxes.

A prototype is a labelled point in feature space. It need not be one of the training points. To classify x, find the nearest prototype and copy its label. Where should the prototypes go? The simplest answer is k-means clustering, run separately inside each class: give every class R prototypes, place them with k-means on that class's points alone, then label each centre with its class. Change R, then press Step to watch Lloyd's algorithm move the centres. Click the plot to drop a query point.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\hat G(x) = g_{j^*} \\ &j^* = \arg\min_{j}\ \lVert x - m_j \rVert \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: m1, …, mJ are the prototypes and gj is the class attached to mj. Find the prototype nearest to x and predict its class. Every point of the plane belongs to the cell of its nearest prototype, so the decision boundary is made of pieces of the perpendicular bisectors between prototypes of different classes.
Say it“G-hat of x is the class of the prototype m-j-star, the one that minimises the distance from x.”
\[ \begin{aligned} &\min_{m_1,\dots,m_R} \sum_{i:\,g_i=k} \min_{r} \lVert x_i - m_r \rVert^2 \\ &m_r \leftarrow \operatorname{mean}\{x_i \text{ nearest } m_r\} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: inside class k, choose R centres so that the points are, in total, as close as possible to their nearest centre. Lloyd's algorithm alternates two steps: give each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points. The total never goes up, so it settles, though possibly in a local minimum.
Say it“Minimise, over the R centres, the sum over class k's points of the squared distance to the nearest centre; then move each centre to the mean of its points.”
Lloyd step

Using the labels

Learning vector quantisation

k-means places each class's prototypes while looking at that class alone. It never sees the other classes, so it has no idea where the boundary is, and that is exactly where prototypes matter most. Teuvo Kohonen's learning vector quantisation (LVQ) fixes this with a simple online rule. Take one training point. Find its nearest prototype. If their classes agree, pull the prototype a little towards the point; if they disagree, push it a little away. Repeat over the data many times while the step size ε shrinks to zero. Prototypes get pushed away from regions where other classes live. Start from k-means, then press One step a few times, then One epoch.

\[ \begin{aligned} &j = \arg\min_{l} \lVert x_i - m_l \rVert \\ &m_j \leftarrow \begin{cases} m_j + \varepsilon\,(x_i - m_j) & g_j = g_i \\[2pt] m_j - \varepsilon\,(x_i - m_j) & g_j \ne g_i \end{cases} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: only the winner, the prototype mj nearest to xi, moves. It moves a fraction ε of the way towards xi when they share a class, and the same fraction away when they don't. ε falls to zero over the run (here linearly), so the prototypes settle. LVQ is defined by this recipe rather than by a criterion it minimises, which makes its properties hard to analyse. Variants LVQ2 and LVQ3 move the two nearest prototypes when xi falls near the midway line between them.
Say it“Move the winning prototype m-j by epsilon times x-i minus m-j: towards the point if the labels match, away from it if they don't.”
epochs done
training error
test error now

A comparative study

k-NN, k-means and LVQ in ten dimensions

How do the three methods compare once they are tuned? Take ten features, each uniform on [0, 1], and two ways of labelling the points. In the easy problem only the first feature matters. In the difficult one the class is a three-dimensional checkerboard: it depends on the first three features jointly, and no single feature on its own tells you anything. The other features are noise in both. We draw 100 training points and 1,000 test points, ten times over, and plot the average test error against the method's size: the number of neighbours k for k-NN, the prototypes per class R for k-means and LVQ. Switch problems and slide along the curves.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{easy:} \quad Y = I\big(X_1 > \tfrac12\big) \\ &\text{difficult:} \\ &\quad Y = I\Big(\textstyle\prod_{j=1}^{3}\big(X_j - \tfrac12\big) > 0\Big) \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: I(·) is 1 when the statement is true and 0 otherwise. In the easy problem the boundary is the flat wall X1 = ½. In the difficult one, cut the cube in half along each of the first three features; the eight small cubes alternate between the classes like a three-dimensional chessboard. Neither rule has noise, so the best possible error is 0; what we see is the cost of learning from 100 points in ten dimensions.
Say it“Easy: Y is one when X-one is above a half. Difficult: Y is one when the product of X-j minus a half, for j from one to three, is positive.”

Example: image scene classification

Neighbours in a satellite image

In the STATLOG project (Michie, Spiegelhalter & Taylor, 1994) dozens of classifiers were run on the same benchmarks. One was a patch of farmland in Australia seen by a Landsat satellite in four spectral bands: two visible (green, red) and two near-infrared. Each pixel, about 80 m across, was labelled on the ground as one of six land types. The features for a pixel are its four band values and those of its eight neighbours: 9 × 4 = 36 numbers. Of all the methods tried, including LVQ, decision trees and neural networks, k-nearest neighbours had the lowest test error. Here is the real data from the UCI repository: 4,435 training pixels and 2,000 test pixels. Compare the centre pixel alone with its whole neighbourhood, and step through the test pixels.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\hat G(x_0) = \arg\max_{g} \sum_{i \in N_k(x_0)} I(g_i = g) \\ &x_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{36} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: find the k training pixels whose 36 numbers are closest to the test pixel's (ordinary Euclidean distance), count their labels, and predict the most common one. The neighbourhood features let the method see texture and edges, not only colour: a pixel of cotton beside a field boundary looks different from one in mid-field.
Say it“G-hat of x-nought is the class g with the most votes among the k nearest neighbours of x-nought.”
test error
this pixel

Checked against numpy: every error count above matches a reference that, like the page, breaks distance ties by training order. Many pixels have exactly tied distances (some patches even appear twice), and scikit-learn breaks those ties differently, so it reports a few more errors with the centre pixel alone: 334 and 322 for k = 3 and 5, against 332 and 319 here. With all 36 features they agree.

Invariant metrics

Tangent distance: ignoring small turns and shifts

Nearest neighbours is only as good as its distance. Take a handwritten 4 and turn it by 15°. To a person it is the same 4. To Euclidean distance, which compares the images pixel by pixel, it may now be farther from the original than some other digit is. We would like a distance that is invariant to small rotations, shifts and changes of size.

As you turn an image through every angle, it traces a curve through the 64-dimensional space of 8 × 8 images. The ideal distance between two digits would be the shortest distance between their curves (or surfaces, with several transformations). That is hard to compute, and it is too forgiving: turn a 6 far enough and it becomes a 9. Simard, LeCun and Denker (1993) replaced each curve by its tangent line at the image: x + a·t, where t says how every pixel changes as the turn begins. A line is easy to work with, and it only covers small turns. Choose a transformation and drag the amount: compare the real transformed digit with the tangent approximation, and watch the two distances.

\[ \begin{aligned} &x(\theta) \approx x + \theta\, t_{\text{rot}} \\ &t_{\text{rot}}[p] = v_p\,\partial_u x[p] - u_p\,\partial_v x[p] \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: a slightly turned image is the original plus a small multiple θ (in radians) of a tangent image. For pixel p at position (up, vp) from the centre, the tangent combines the image's horizontal and vertical gradients ∂ux and ∂vx (measured on a lightly blurred copy). Shifts use the gradients alone; scaling uses up∂ux + vp∂vx. These are the chain rule applied to “move the pixels”.
Say it“x of theta is about x plus theta times the rotation tangent, which at pixel p is v-p times the horizontal gradient minus u-p times the vertical gradient.”
\[ \begin{aligned} d_T(x, p) &= \min_{a} \lVert x - p - T_p\, a \rVert^2 \\ &= \lVert x - p\rVert^2 - \lVert Q_p^{\top}(x - p)\rVert^2 \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: Tp holds p's tangent images as columns (here four: shift right, shift down, rotate, scale), so p + Tpa is every small transformation of p at once, a flat 4-dimensional sheet. dT is the squared distance from x to the nearest point of that sheet. With Qp an orthonormal basis of the sheet, it is the ordinary squared distance minus the part of x − p the sheet can explain. This one-sided version uses p's tangents only; the two-sided version also moves x along its own sheet.
Say it“The tangent distance from x to p is the smallest squared distance from x to p plus T-p times a, over all a.”

Adaptive nearest neighbours

DANN: neighbourhoods that follow the boundary

k-NN assumes the class probabilities are roughly constant across the neighbourhood. Near a boundary they are not: they change quickly across the boundary and hardly at all along it. A round neighbourhood that straddles the boundary mixes the classes. In many dimensions the problem is worse, because the neighbourhood has to reach a long way out to find k points. A better neighbourhood is a slab or ellipse, thin across the boundary and long along it.

Hastie and Tibshirani's discriminant adaptive nearest neighbours (DANN) builds that ellipse at each query. Take the 50 points nearest to x0. Measure how spread out each class is (the pooled within-class covariance W) and how far apart the class means are (the between-class covariance B). Then shrink the directions in which the means differ. Below, the orange class fills a disc and the teal class surrounds it. Drag the query star around the circle and watch the ellipse turn to lie along the boundary.

\[ \begin{aligned} &D(x, x_0) = (x - x_0)^{\top}\, \Sigma\, (x - x_0) \\ &\Sigma = W^{-1/2}\,\big[\,B^{*} + \varepsilon I\,\big]\, W^{-1/2} \\ &B^{*} = W^{-1/2} B\, W^{-1/2} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: first sphere the data with W−1/2, so each class's local spread is round. In the sphered space, B* = W−1/2BW−1/2 is large along the line joining the class means: distances along it are stretched, so the neighbourhood is squeezed in that direction. Without ε the neighbourhood would be an infinitely long strip along the boundary; εI rounds its ends into an ellipse. Hastie and Tibshirani suggest ε = 1 and 50 local points.
Say it“The distance is x minus x-nought, transposed, times Sigma, times x minus x-nought; Sigma is W to the minus a half, times B-star plus epsilon I, times W to the minus a half.”
\[ \begin{aligned} W &= \textstyle\sum_{k} \pi_k W_k \\ B &= \textstyle\sum_{k} \pi_k\, (\bar x_k - \bar x)(\bar x_k - \bar x)^{\top} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: both are computed from the 50 local points only. πk is the share of them in class k, Wk is class k's covariance among them, x̄k its mean, and x̄ the mean of all 50. Where the 50 points are all one class, B = 0 and DANN falls back to an ordinary round neighbourhood (after sphering).
Say it“W is the sum over classes of pi-k times W-k. B is the sum of pi-k times the outer product of x-bar-k minus x-bar with itself.”
k-NN vote
DANN vote
ellipse length : width

Example: a shell in ten dimensions

Here is a test in the spirit of Hastie and Tibshirani's own. Both classes are ten-dimensional standard normal points, but one class is only kept when its squared length lies between 22.4 and 40: a thin shell that wraps all the way round the other class. We draw 250 points per class for training and 250 per class for testing, five times over. Plain 5-NN struggles because a point on the shell is often closer to the dense middle than to the other, sparse shell points. DANN stretches each neighbourhood along the shell. Press Run (it takes about a second).

Global dimension reduction

One subspace for all the neighbourhoods

DANN finds the important directions afresh at every query. Often the same few directions matter everywhere, and the rest are noise. Then we can find them once: compute the local between-class matrix Bi at every training point, average them, and keep the leading eigenvectors of the average. Nearest neighbours in that small subspace ignores the noise features altogether. In the problem below only two of ten features matter: the orange class is a disc in the first two, the teal class surrounds it, and the other eight features are pure noise of the same size. Slide L, the number of directions kept.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\bar B = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} B_i = \sum_{l=1}^{p} \theta_l\, e_l e_l^{\top} \\ &\min_{\operatorname{rank}(M)=L}\ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \operatorname{tr}\big[(B_i - M)^2\big] \\ &\Rightarrow\ M = \sum_{l=1}^{L} \theta_l\, e_l e_l^{\top} \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: Bi is DANN's between-class matrix computed in the neighbourhood of training point i. Average them and take the eigen-decomposition: el are the eigenvectors and θl ≥ 0 the eigenvalues, largest first. Among all rank-L matrices, the one closest to every Bi at once (in total squared error) keeps just the top L eigenvectors. So project the data onto e1, …, eL and run k-NN there.
Say it“B-bar is the average of the local between matrices; the best rank-L summary of all of them keeps the top L eigenvectors of B-bar.”
5-NN test error, L directions
5-NN, all ten features

Computational considerations

Editing, condensing and fast search

Nearest neighbours does no work at training time and all of it at prediction time. Finding the nearest of N stored points in p dimensions by brute force costs about N·p operations per query, and all N points must be kept. Three remedies help. Fast search: a kd-tree splits the space in half again and again and skips whole boxes that cannot hold anything closer than the best point found so far (Friedman, Bentley & Finkel, 1977). It works well in a few dimensions and loses its edge in many. Editing removes training points that their neighbours misclassify, cleaning the overlap between the classes; the multi-edit algorithm repeatedly splits the data into parts and edits each part using the next. Condensing (Hart, 1968) keeps only the points needed to classify the rest correctly: start with one point and add any point the current store gets wrong. Points deep inside a class are never needed. Press Multi-edit, then Condense, and click the plot to watch a kd-tree search.

\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{brute force:} \quad N\,p \\ &\text{kd-tree, small } p\text{:} \quad \approx c^{\,p} \log N \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: brute force compares the query with all N points, p coordinates each. A kd-tree descends about log2N levels to a first candidate, then checks only the boxes that could hold something closer. In low dimensions that is a few dozen distance calculations whatever N is. The number of nearby boxes grows quickly with p, so in many dimensions the savings fade.
Say it“Brute force costs N times p per query; a kd-tree costs roughly a constant to the power p times log N.”
\[ \begin{aligned} &\text{add } x_i \text{ to } S \\ &\text{if } \hat G_S(x_i) \ne g_i \end{aligned} \]
Read it as: S is the growing store, and ĜS is 1-NN using only the points in S. Sweep through the training points in random order, adding each one the store misclassifies, and sweep again until a full pass adds nothing. Then 1-NN on S classifies every training point correctly, with far fewer points. Condensing keeps noise points too, which is why editing comes first.
Say it“Add x-i to the store S whenever 1-NN on S gets its label wrong.”
points stored

Real-world project

Project: reading handwritten digits with LVQ and tangent distance

The UCI Optical Recognition of Handwritten Digits data (Alpaydin & Kaynak, 1998) comes from forms filled in by 43 people. Each digit was scanned as a 32 × 32 black-and-white bitmap, then cut into 4 × 4 blocks; each of the 8 × 8 = 64 features counts the inked pixels in one block, from 0 to 16. The 3,823 training digits come from 30 writers and the 1,797 test digits from 13 other writers, so the test really is new handwriting.

The plan has three steps. Place R prototypes per digit with k-means. Polish them with five epochs of LVQ (ε0 = 0.1). Then classify every test digit by its nearest prototype, under Euclidean and under tangent distance. As yardsticks, run 1-NN against all 3,823 training digits with both distances. Everything runs in your browser; the full tangent-distance 1-NN takes a few seconds. Choose R and press Train.

The prototypes themselves

Each row is one digit's R prototypes after LVQ. They are averages of many handwritten digits, so they look like blurred, idealised digits, and the different prototypes of a class capture different styles: a 1 with or without a base, a 7 with or without a cross-bar.

Inspect a test digit

Why does tangent distance help? For one test digit, see its nearest prototype under each distance, and the prototype after it has been slid along its tangent sheet to match the test digit as closely as small shifts, a turn and a change of size allow.

The same project in Python

import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

tr = np.loadtxt("optdigits.tra", delimiter=",", dtype=int)   # UCI: 3,823 training digits
te = np.loadtxt("optdigits.tes", delimiter=",", dtype=int)   #      1,797 test digits
Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte = tr[:, :64].astype(float), tr[:, 64], te[:, :64].astype(float), te[:, 64]

def mulberry32(a):                      # the page's random generator, so both make the same choices
    s = [a & 0xFFFFFFFF]
    def r():
        s[0] = (s[0] + 0x6D2B79F5) & 0xFFFFFFFF; t = s[0]
        t = (t ^ (t >> 15)) * (1 | t) & 0xFFFFFFFF
        t = ((t + ((t ^ (t >> 7)) * (61 | t) & 0xFFFFFFFF)) & 0xFFFFFFFF) ^ t
        return (t ^ (t >> 14)) / 4294967296
    return r

def kmeans(X, R, seed):                 # k-means++ start, then Lloyd until nothing moves
    r = mulberry32(seed); C = [X[int(r() * len(X))]]
    while len(C) < R:
        d2 = ((X[:, None] - np.array(C)[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).min(1)
        C.append(X[np.searchsorted(np.cumsum(d2), r() * d2.sum(), side="right")])
    C, a = np.array(C), None
    for _ in range(100):
        b = ((X[:, None] - C[None]) ** 2).sum(-1).argmin(1)
        if a is not None and (a == b).all(): break
        a = b; C = np.array([X[a == j].mean(0) if (a == j).any() else C[j] for j in range(R)])
    return C

def lvq1(M, L, X, y, epochs=5, eps0=0.1, seed=7):   # LVQ1, learning rate falling linearly to 0
    M, r, T, t = M.copy(), mulberry32(seed), epochs * len(X), 0
    for _ in range(epochs):
        p = list(range(len(X)))
        for i in range(len(p) - 1, 0, -1): j = int(r() * (i + 1)); p[i], p[j] = p[j], p[i]
        for i in p:
            j = ((M - X[i]) ** 2).sum(1).argmin(); eps = eps0 * (1 - t / T); t += 1
            M[j] += (eps if L[j] == y[i] else -eps) * (X[i] - M[j])
    return M

def tangents(P, s=0.6):                 # x-shift, y-shift, rotation, scaling of each 8x8 image
    g = np.exp(-np.arange(-2, 3) ** 2 / (2 * s * s)); g /= g.sum()
    B = P.reshape(-1, 8, 8)
    for ax in (2, 1): B = sum(w * np.roll(np.pad(B, ((0, 0), (2, 2), (2, 2))), k, ax)[:, 2:-2, 2:-2] for k, w in zip(range(-2, 3), g))
    Z = np.pad(B, ((0, 0), (1, 1), (1, 1)))
    gx, gy = (Z[:, 1:-1, 2:] - Z[:, 1:-1, :-2]) / 2, (Z[:, 2:, 1:-1] - Z[:, :-2, 1:-1]) / 2
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[0:8, 0:8] - 3.5
    T = np.stack([gx, gy, yy * gx - xx * gy, xx * gx + yy * gy], -1).reshape(-1, 64, 4)
    return np.linalg.qr(T)[0]           # an orthonormal basis of each tangent plane

def nearest(Xq, P, Q=None):             # Euclidean, or one-sided tangent distance if Q is given
    out = []
    for s in range(0, len(Xq), 100):
        D = Xq[s:s + 100, None] - P[None]; d = (D ** 2).sum(-1)
        if Q is not None: d = d - (np.einsum("qnd,ndt->qnt", D, Q) ** 2).sum(-1)
        out.append(d.argmin(1))
    return np.concatenate(out)

def report(name, n, pred): e = int((pred != yte).sum()); print(f"{name:34s} stored {n:5d}   errors {e:3d}   test error {100 * e / len(yte):.2f}%")

report("1-NN, Euclidean", len(Xtr), ytr[nearest(Xte, Xtr)])
report("1-NN, scikit-learn (check)", len(Xtr), KNeighborsClassifier(1).fit(Xtr, ytr).predict(Xte))
report("1-NN, tangent distance", len(Xtr), ytr[nearest(Xte, Xtr, tangents(Xtr))])
for R in (1, 3, 5, 10, 20):
    P = np.vstack([kmeans(Xtr[ytr == c], R, 100 + c) for c in range(10)]); L = np.repeat(np.arange(10), R)
    M = lvq1(P, L, Xtr, ytr)
    report(f"k-means, R={R}, Euclidean", len(P), L[nearest(Xte, P)])
    report(f"k-means, R={R}, tangent", len(P), L[nearest(Xte, P, tangents(P))])
    report(f"LVQ,     R={R}, Euclidean", len(M), L[nearest(Xte, M)])
    report(f"LVQ,     R={R}, tangent", len(M), L[nearest(Xte, M, tangents(M))])

The page runs the same algorithms with the same random generator, so it makes the same random choices as the Python script, and every error count in the table above matches the output exactly. Two honest notes. First, LVQ does not help on this data. The digit classes are well separated, so the k-means prototypes already sit in sensible places, and LVQ changes the error count by only a handful either way; with Euclidean distance it is slightly worse at most R. We tried other step sizes and epoch counts offline and found no setting that helps consistently. The big, reliable gains come from more prototypes and from tangent distance. Second, the tangent distance is one-sided and unpenalised, with four transformations on coarse 8 × 8 images. Simard and colleagues used seven transformations on 16 × 16 images, two-sided, with smoothing, and their gains on postal digits were larger than the drop from 36 to 26 errors seen here.

Wrap-up

Five lines to remember

  • A prototype classifier stores a few labelled points and gives each new case the label of the nearest one; k-means run inside each class is the simplest way to place them.
  • LVQ uses the labels: the winning prototype is pulled towards points of its own class and pushed away from others, with a step size that shrinks to zero.
  • Nearest neighbours is only as good as its distance. Tangent distance measures from x to the flat sheet of small shifts, turns and rescalings of p, so it ignores the changes that do not alter a digit's meaning.
  • DANN reshapes each neighbourhood with local within- and between-class covariances: thin across the boundary, long along it. Averaging the local between-class matrices gives a global subspace for k-NN.
  • The cost is at prediction time, N·p per query: kd-trees speed up search in low dimensions, editing cleans the overlap and condensing keeps only the points near the boundary.

Check your understanding

Why can k-means prototypes be badly placed for classification, even when k-means itself works perfectly?

k-means places each class's prototypes using that class's points alone, to summarise them well. It never looks at the other classes, so it ignores where the boundary is. A prototype in a region shared with another class can then claim points that belong to the other class. LVQ fixes this by pushing prototypes away from points of other classes.

In LVQ, what happens to a prototype that keeps winning points of a different class?

Each such win pushes it a step ε away from that point. It drifts out of the region where the other class lives, until the points it wins are mostly its own class, or until ε has shrunk to zero.

Why not use the exact invariant distance, the shortest distance between the full rotation curves of two digits?

It is expensive to compute, and it is too invariant: large rotations change meaning (a 6 turned through 180° becomes a 9). The tangent line only covers small transformations, and it reduces the problem to a small least-squares fit.

At a query point where all 50 local points are one class, what does the DANN metric become?

All class means equal the overall mean, so B = 0 and Σ = W−1/2(εI)W−1/2 = εW−1. The neighbourhood is an ordinary ellipse shaped by the local spread of the data, with no stretching along a boundary, which is sensible because there is no boundary nearby.

You condense a noisy training set without editing it first. Why is the result disappointing?

Condensing keeps every point the store misclassifies, and noise points (points sitting among the other class) are always misclassified, so they are all kept. The store stays large, and the 1-NN boundary still bends around every noise point. Editing first removes them.
